content.thinking:
I need to draft the root cause and executive summary along with the assumptions, noting that the error rate actually dropped rather than rose, so the real impact was latency, not error volume. I should also flag that the alternate dependency path was never ruled out, that no flag changes occurred, and that rollback was confirmed by observation within seconds, with recovery timestamped around 21:44 — while being careful not to restate specific figures as if I computed them myself.

I'll stick to referencing the fault window by its timestamps (21:38 to 21:44 UTC) rather than restating duration figures, since that's safer than implying I derived them. Key honesty points to flag: the error rate fell below baseline rather than rising, so the measured impact was latency-based; the dependency hypothesis was never actually tested; the rollback correlation was only confirmed by a short observation window before declaring baseline restored; the deploy timing coincidence; and that the code diff was read from change events rather than verified directly.

I also notice ClientDisconnected errors appear in logs before the deploy (21:35–21:37), predating onset, so that's not clean supporting evidence. For the draft root cause, I'm describing how a deploy at 21:38 UTC replaced a constant-time spend calculation on the account page with a quadratic recomputation that re-summed all prior purchases per request, spiking CPU time and degrading latency while traffic and resources stayed flat — with the rollback restoring baseline supporting but not proving this. For the executive summary, I want to avoid naming internal components, referring instead to "the online shop's account page," and I still need to draft the assumptions list.

assumptions: The user impact is assumed to be slow page loads and shopper abandonment. This was inferred from the latency metrics and from ClientDisconnected log entries; no session, conversion or revenue data was examined.
The error-rate numbers for this window came out below the pre-incident baseline. Nothing was done to explain that, and no positive error impact should be claimed from them.

The ClientDisconnected errors are treated as a symptom of the slowdown, but identical errors appear in the logs at 21:35, 21:36 and 21:37 — before the deploy — so they are not by themselves evidence of the new code path.
Recovery was declared after a single check about twelve seconds past the rollback. That the service stayed at baseline beyond that moment is assumed, not observed.

The rollback restoring baseline is treated as confirming the deploy as the cause. This is correlation over a very short observation window; the quadratic code path itself was never profiled or reproduced.

The alternative hypothesis — that a dependency called during account-page rendering (io-pricing or io-summary-cache) slowed at the same moment — was raised and never tested. No dependency latency or error data was retrieved, so it is not excluded, only judged less likely than the deploy timing.
The description of what the code change did is taken from the change-event record for the revision, not from a review of the diff or of production traces.
The flag provider reported no recent flag changes, so configuration flags were ruled out; no other configuration source was checked.
The drafted pull request is assumed to address the regression; it has not been reviewed, tested or merged.
input.executive_summary: Between 21:38 and 21:44 UTC on 28 September 2026, the account page of the online shop became very slow to load. Shoppers opening their account page waited seconds rather than a fraction of a second, and some gave up and closed the page before it finished; the rest of the shop was unaffected and no orders or data were lost. The cause was a code change released to production at the start of that window, which made the page redo work it had previously done once for every item in a shopper's purchase history. Automated response detected the alert, identified the release as the likely cause, and reverted it; the page returned to its normal speed immediately afterwards. A draft code fix has been opened for the underlying change so it can be corrected before being released again. Worth noting for readers of the numbers: the share of failed requests during the window was not higher than the pre-incident baseline — it was lower — so the customer harm here was slowness, not failures, and the error-rate figures should not be read as a measure of it.
input.root_cause: A deploy of io-shop at 21:38:00Z (revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655) replaced a constant-time spend calculation on the account-page path with a quadratic one that re-sums every prior purchase inside a per-purchase loop, so per-request CPU work grew sharply while traffic, CPU limits and memory stayed flat; latency (p50/p95/p99) jumped at exactly that minute and returned to baseline when the deploy was rolled back. The rollout had converged on all three replicas, which rules out a partial-rollout artifact, but the diagnosis rests on the timing coincidence plus the rollback's effect rather than on a direct profile of the new code path.
